title: Machine-learning-guided CsrA homolog screens reveal divergent bacterial regulatory activities
summary: A Swarm-seq assay tested more than 500 bacterial CsrA homologs for regulation of Bacillus subtilis swarming and found two functional classes: several homologs strongly inhibited swarming while others failed despite conserved sequence and canonical GGA motifs in the hag transcript. A random-forest model trained on these assays predicted homolog activity across thousands of sequences; experimental testing supported predicted Class I regulatory activity for Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus CsrA and Pseudomonas putida RsmA. The findings indicate sequence conservation and the canonical RNA motif do not alone determine these tested regulatory effects.
ai_technology: Random-forest machine-learning classifier trained on Swarm-seq functional assay data

evidence.tested: A Swarm-seq assay tested more than 500 bacterial CsrA homologs for regulation of Bacillus subtilis swarming and found two functional classes: several homologs strongly inhibited swarming while others failed despite conserved sequence and canonical GGA motifs in the hag transcript.
evidence.unknown: Activity classifications are based on the reported B. subtilis swarming assay and tested proteins; they do not establish all native targets or regulatory functions in each source organism. The predicted function landscape across thousands of homologs is not experimentally validated wholesale. Primary publisher abstract checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: High-throughput swarming assays generated a functional dataset; machine learning was then trained to classify homolog functional activity across the bacterial domain and nominate homologs for validation. Selected CsrABb and RsmAPp predictions were experimentally validated.
